question: What will the US unemployment rate be for September 2026, as reported by the BLS on October 2, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Prior from the reference class: one-month U-3 changes in non-recession months have near-zero drift and SD ~0.10-0.11pp, so the random-walk anchor is August's unrounded 4.141% (7031/169777), not the rounded 4.1. That placement is decisive: the level is 0.009pp from the 4.15 cut, so a literally flat month still prints 4.1 but any small rise prints 4.2. Adjusting off the anchor: four months of downward drift (4.337->4.296->4.189->4.090) argue lower, as do claims at 196k with continuing claims 1.73M (lowest since Jan 2024), Challenger YTD cuts at a four-year low, and a labor force down 973k y/y that mechanically suppresses the rate; against that, August's +0.05 reversal, a 12-month payroll trend of only ~31k/mo, weak ADP (+38k), and AI-driven information-sector losses argue higher. Net: median ~4.13, slightly below the anchor. Exact-match Polymarket contracts (thin, $1-4k volume) normalize to ~0.36/0.32/0.16/0.11 on 4.1/4.2/4.0/4.3, closely matching my independent fit. The Sept 6-12 reference week and its collection week are already closed, so residual uncertainty is sampling and seasonal-adjustment noise, not news; a shutdown delay is off the table (CR funds through Dec 11) and would not change the value anyway per the fine print. AskNews items describing a December report at 4.4% are mis-stamped Dec-2025 data and were discarded.

calls.reference_class: One-month changes in the seasonally adjusted U-3 unemployment rate (first print) during non-recession expansion months, conditioned on the prior month's UNROUNDED rate rather than its rounded print

calls.reasoning: Anchor is the unrounded August 2026 level, 7,031k/169,777k = 4.141% (BLS Table A-1), not the rounded 4.1 headline. From that anchor the rounding bands are badly asymmetric: only +0.009pp rounds up to 4.2, while -0.091pp is needed to reach 4.0. With a random walk of sigma ~0.10pp/month this yields roughly 4.1 ~36%, 4.2 ~31%, 4.0 ~16%, 4.3 ~11%, tails ~6%. Drift set a whisker below zero: the Sept 6-12 CPS reference week saw initial claims fall to 196k and continuing claims hit a 2-year low (1.774M), and 2026's trend has been downward (4.4 Feb -> 4.1 Jul/Aug) on shrinking labor supply; offsetting that, August's unrounded rate rose 0.05pp, the level sits at the bottom of the 2026 range, and information-sector job losses are a live upward risk. The exact-terms Polymarket bucket book (normalized: 4.1 .34, 4.2 .30, 4.0 .15, 4.3 .11, ~$14.5k volume, 16% overround and an incoherent 4.4/4.5 tail) matches my model closely, so I blended ~50/50 and smoothed its noisy tails. Critically, the reference week is already fully elapsed - the number exists and is merely unpublished - so no widening for future news is warranted. No escape mass: exiting 3.65-4.65 requires a one-month move of +/-0.5pp, unprecedented outside 2020.

- Dispersion, over one-month horizons: SD of the change in the unrounded rate is ~0.085pp across Mar-Aug 2026 and ~0.10-0.12pp across the broader 2015-2019 / 2023-2026 window.
- Over the last 12 same-length (one-month) windows: the rounded rate moved by a tenth or more in 7 of 12 and was unchanged in 5 of 12 (Nov-2025 4.5 through Aug-2026 4.1, FRED UNRATE).

calls.reasoning: Anchor: the unrounded U-3 implied by Table A-1 for Aug 2026 is 7,031/169,777 = 4.14%, sitting just 0.01pp under the 4.15 boundary that prints 4.2 and 0.09pp above the 4.05 boundary that prints 4.0 - so 4.1 and 4.2 are close to coin-flip neighbours and the distribution is skewed toward 4.0 rather than 4.3 only mildly. Reference class (one-month-ahead U-3 in a low-volatility regime) gives SD ~0.12pp, essentially all sampling noise plus small true drift. Direction of drift is genuinely two-sided: claims in the Sept 6-12 CPS reference week were 196k with continuing claims at a two-year low and participation still eroding (both push down), while the rate already ticked up in unrounded terms Jul->Aug, August's 683k labor-force surge signals re-entry that can outrun an ~80k/month hiring pace, and 2026 payroll revisions have skewed negative (both push up). I therefore kept the center essentially at the August level with no meaningful drift. RESOLUTION INSTRUMENT: resolves off the FIRST published BLS Employment Situation for September 2026 (Oct 2, 2026, 8:30 a.m. ET, bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm), seasonally adjusted U-3, to one decimal place - NOT off later revisions, NOT off the annual benchmark/seasonal-factor revisions (those land with the January report), and NOT off the establishment-survey payroll number. EVENT WINDOW: the criteria fix the measured month as September 2026. The CPS household-survey reference week is the week containing the 12th -> Sept 6-12, 2026, with collection the following week (Sept 13-19). As of Now (2026-09-21T18:00:21Z) that window is 100% elapsed and collection is complete; the figure exists and is unpublished, so no post-Now economic news can alter it.

EVIDENCE
- BLS Employment Situation for Aug 2026, released 2026-09-04: U-3 4.1% seasonally adjusted, unchanged from July; unemployed 7,031k; civilian labor force 169,777k; LFPR 61.6%; employment-population ratio 59.1%; nonfarm payrolls +162,000. (bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm)
- Consensus going into that August report was +53,000 payrolls and 4.1% unemployment; payrolls beat substantially, the rate was in line. (CNBC, 2026-09-04)
- Unrounded rates computed from BLS Table A-1 levels (bls.gov/news.release/empsit.t01.htm): Jun 2026 7,094/169,358 = 4.19%; Jul 2026 6,916/169,094 = 4.09%; Aug 2026 7,031/169,777 = 4.14%. The reported Aug value of 4.1 therefore sits about 0.01pp below the 4.15 cut that would print 4.2, and about 0.09pp above the 4.05 cut that would print 4.0.
- Published 2026 rounded path: May 4.3, Jun 4.2, Jul 4.1, Aug 4.1; Aug 2025 was 4.3; the 2026 high was 4.4 early in the year. No single published month-over-month move in this stretch exceeded 0.1pp. (BLS Table A-1; Trading Economics)
- In August the civilian labor force rose 683,000 and employment rose 569,000; LFPR went 61.4 -> 61.6. Over the longer arc LFPR is down about 0.5pp since January 2026 and about 0.7pp from Aug 2025's 62.3% - a shrinking denominator that has been a mechanical drag on the rate independent of hiring. (BLS)
- U-6 fell to 7.7% in August from 7.9% in July. (Trading Economics, 2026-09-04)
- Initial jobless claims, week ending Sept 12, 2026 (the CPS reference week): 196,000, down 10,000 from 206,000, versus market expectations of 208,000, and the lowest since the 189,000 print in July. Continuing claims 1,730,000, lowest since January 2024. (Washington Times 2026-09-17; Trading Economics)
- 2026 hiring pace to date has averaged roughly 80,000 jobs/month, versus roughly 9,700/month in 2025 and roughly 166,000/month across 2023-2024. (Trading Economics, Sept 2026)
- Trading Economics' own next-release model forecast is 4.1%, with its longer-run path drifting toward 4.3% by end-Q3 2026 and 4.3% in 2027.

BASE RATES AND DISPERSION
- Over ALL months: BLS states the 90% confidence interval on the month-to-month change in the unemployment rate is about +/-0.2 percentage point, implying an SD of roughly 0.12pp per month on the unrounded rate from sampling error alone. This is the unconditional figure across all regimes.
- CONDITIONAL on a non-recessionary, low-layoff regime (2015-2019, 2023-2026 - the condition that holds here, given claims near multi-decade lows): realized rounded month-over-month changes are 0.0 or +/-0.1 in the overwhelming majority of months, and the realized SD of unrounded monthly changes runs nearer 0.10pp than 0.12pp. The two 2026 changes I can compute directly are -0.10pp (Jun->Jul) and +0.05pp (Jul->Aug).
- CONDITIONAL on the starting unrounded rate sitting within 0.02pp of a rounding boundary (as here): the reported value is close to a coin flip between the two adjacent tenths regardless of which way the underlying rate drifts - the rounding geometry, not the economics, dominates.
- Event-in-window count: across the published 2026 monthly series I could retrieve, zero one-month windows contained a reported move of 0.2pp or more.

EVIDENCE POINTING DOWN: claims at or near 60-year lows in the reference week; continuing claims at a two-year low; participation and labor force still structurally eroding through 2026; August payrolls beat consensus by more than 100k; the rate has already fallen 0.3pp from the 2026 high.
EVIDENCE POINTING UP: the unrounded rate already rose Jul->Aug (4.09 -> 4.14); August's 683k labor-force surge indicates re-entry that an ~80k/month average hiring pace may not absorb; the 2026 hiring pace is less than half the 2023-24 average; payroll revisions through 2026 have repeatedly been negative.

SCHEDULE RISK: federal funding is in place through December 11, 2026, and the BLS October 2026 schedule lists the release for Oct 2; no announced delay was found.

It is not evidence about September 2026.

FACTUAL disputes settled internally: (a) the continuing-claims figure - Run 2's reasoning called 1.774M a two-year low, but its own dossier dates 1,774k to the week ended Aug 29, while Runs 1 and 3 give 1,730k for the reference-week-adjacent report of Sept 17; I use 1,730k, and the direction is unaffected either way. (b) the Polymarket quote - Run 3's raw 40c vs Runs 1-2's normalized 34-36c is arithmetic, not contradiction: the harness ladder (4.1 .39 / 4.2 .34 / 4.0 .17 / 4.3 .12 / <=3.8 .01) omits the 3.9, 4.4 and 4.5 buckets, so the book sums to ~1.05-1.08 and normalizes to ~.36/.31/.16/.11, implying a center near 4.14. (c) contract match - only Run 3 verified the rules text against source/month/initial-release-only/one-decimal; I accept that, with the caveat that ~$14.5k volume and a 4.4-quoted-below-4.5 tail make it evidence rather than an anchor. (d) All three independently searched for and failed to find a post-Sept-10 economist consensus for this print, and all three independently flagged the circulating 'December report at 4.4%' items as misdated Dec-2025 content - I treat both as settled by concurrence and discard the stale items. JUDGMENT disputes, no evidence available to break them: drift (Run 3 zero vs Runs 1-2 slightly negative) and sigma (0.105 vs 0.12). I take drift modestly negative because the reference-week claims data is the most window-relevant hard evidence there is, but hold it small because the market's own implied center says zero drift and the August labor-force outlier is an upward-reverting risk; sigma I set at 0.11, between the BLS-stated ~0.12 and the realized 2026 ~0.08. I carry forward the runs' shared reference class (random walk off the unrounded 4.141, not the rounded headline) because it is correct and decisive here. My median of 4.13 sits inside the runs' 4.13-4.14 span not by splitting it but because the reconciled evidence - a genuine but small downward pull, capped by an exact-terms market implying none - puts it there.

disagreements.claim: Escape mass past the 3.65 / 4.65 open bounds should be declared
disagreements.verdict: All three declared none and I agree: a +/-0.5pp one-month move is unprecedented outside 2020, and the survey is already collected. No mechanism, so both fields omitted.

calls.reference_class: One-month changes in the seasonally adjusted U-3 first print during non-recessionary regimes (2015-2019, 2023-2026), applied as a near-zero-drift random walk to the August 2026 UNROUNDED level of 4.141% (7,031k/169,777k, BLS Table A-1), not to the rounded 4.1 headline.
